ann_32.text: This part acts on 116 of 242 training patients (48%), and 77 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with 1 vessel coloured, a flat ST segment, 1.6 mm of ST depression, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy and a reversible thallium defect), the predicted risk is above 99% with or without it, so it changes only slightly (on the training data only).

Through it, more ST depression on exercise raises the predicted risk in an uneven way, adding risk only once it rises above about 1.2 mm (between 0.2 and 1.2 mm for different patients): for a typical patient from about 12% at 0 mm to about 32% at 2.8 mm, and for the typical patient with this bend (a 56-year-old man with signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG), from about 14% at 0 mm to about 51% at 3.5 mm (on the training data only).
Through it, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL and a reversible thallium defect each raise a typical patient's predicted risk from about 12% to about 18% (on the training data only).
More ST depression clearly raises the predicted risk more, in an uneven way, with a reversible thallium defect (from about 27% to about 76%, against about 12% to about 32% without it).

A downsloping ST segment raises it more if fasting blood sugar is 120 mg/dL or less (from about 12% to about 42%, against about 3% to about 10% above 120 mg/dL), but the model has little data on this: only 17 training patients have a downsloping ST segment.

ann_33.text: This part acts on only 19 of 242 training patients (8%), women whose chest pain is brought on by exercise; 12 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 57-year-old woman with chest pain on exercise, a flat ST segment, 1.0 mm of ST depression and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG), it raises the predicted risk from about 9% to about 43% (the model has little data on this; on the training data only).
Through it, chest pain brought on by exercise and being a woman each raise that patient's predicted risk from about 9% to about 43% (on the training data only).
Across the whole model, being a woman lowers the predicted risk slightly more if exercise does not bring on chest pain (from about 12% to below 1%, against about 12% to about 2% with it).

ann_34.text: This part acts on 74 of 242 training patients (31%), and 13 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 51-year-old man with non-anginal chest pain, 0.2 mm of ST depression and a maximum heart rate of 169 beats per minute), it slightly lowers the predicted risk, from about 1% to below 1%.

For the typical patient it acts on, a higher maximum heart rate changes nothing through this part until about 147 beats per minute, then lowers the predicted risk steadily, but only slightly, from about 1% to below 1%, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower (on the training data only).
Non-anginal chest pain and an abnormal thallium scan each change the predicted risk only slightly through it (on the training data only).

A higher maximum heart rate (118 to 175 beats per minute) lowers the predicted risk slowly at first, then faster, and clearly more so with non-anginal chest pain (from about 3% to below 1%, against about 22% to about 8% otherwise), flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower.

A thallium scan that is not normal raises it more if the chest pain is not non-anginal (from about 12% to about 37%, against about 1% to about 4% with non-anginal chest pain; on the training data only).

ann_35.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (below 1%), non-anginal chest pain (about 1%) or atypical angina (about 7%) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 12%).

More vessels coloured raise the predicted risk steadily, each extra vessel adding about the same: a typical patient goes from about 12% at 0 vessels to about 98% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because it cannot go much higher, and a flat ST segment raises it to about 76% and a reversible thallium defect to about 37% (on the training data only).
More ST depression on exercise raises it in an uneven way, from about 12% at 0 mm to about 32% at 2.8 mm (on the training data only).

Higher cholesterol and higher resting blood pressure each raise it steadily: from about 5% at 193 mg/dL to about 31% at 308 mg/dL (flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower), and from about 7% at 110 mm Hg to about 22% at 155 mm Hg (on the training data only).

A higher maximum heart rate lowers it slowly at first, then faster, from about 22% at 118 to about 8% at 175 beats per minute, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower (on the training data only).
Being a woman lowers it to below 1%, and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 3% (on the training data only).

A thallium result coded 4 raises it to about 90% (2 patients) and a fixed defect on the thallium scan lowers it to about 3% (15 patients); the model has little data on this, and both hold on the training data only.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted risk only slightly (on the training data only): older age raises it steadily, from about 10% at 42 to about 13% at 66 years, and a resting ECG that is not normal raises it a little.

The model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if thallium stress test result is something other than a normal thallium scan than if the thallium scan is normal, and even more so if chest pain type is something other than non-anginal chest pain: for a typical patient, going from a normal thallium scan to thallium stress test result other than a normal thallium scan moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 12% to about 37% if chest pain type is something other than non-anginal chest pain, and from about 1% to about 4% if the patient has non-anginal chest pain (on the training data only).
